title: The Logic of the Argumentative Essay
text:
An argumentative essay presents a claim and supports it with evidence. Writers must anticipate objections from readers who hold opposing views. A strong essay acknowledges these counterarguments and responds to them directly. Without this step, the argument may appear one-sided and unconvincing.

Moreover, the choice of evidence matters as much as its quantity. Statistics, expert opinions, and documented examples are generally more persuasive than personal anecdotes alone. Therefore, a writer should select sources carefully and explain how each one supports the central claim.

questions.text: According to paragraph one, what must writers anticipate?
options: Objections from readers who hold opposing views

questions.text: According to paragraph two, which kinds of evidence are generally more persuasive than personal anecdotes alone?
options: Statistics, expert opinions, and documented examples

questions.text: What can be inferred about an essay that ignores counterarguments?
options: It is likely to seem one-sided and less convincing
It will always be rejected by editors
It will be shorter than other essays
It must rely only on statistics

questions.text: Why does the writer recommend explaining how each source supports the central claim?
options: The central claim must be changed
A source without explanation may not clearly strengthen the central claim

vocabulary.definition: to expect something and prepare for it in advance
arguments that oppose a position someone has taken
able to convince someone to believe or do something
short personal stories used as examples

paragraph_translations: Un ensayo argumentativo presenta una tesis y la respalda con pruebas. Los escritores deben anticipar las objeciones de lectores que sostienen puntos de vista opuestos. Un buen ensayo reconoce estos contraargumentos y responde a ellos directamente. Sin este paso, el argumento puede parecer unilateral y poco convincente.

Además, la elección de las pruebas importa tanto como su cantidad. Las estadísticas, las opiniones de expertos y los ejemplos documentados suelen ser más persuasivos que las anécdotas personales por sí solas. Por lo tanto, el escritor debe seleccionar sus fuentes con cuidado y explicar cómo cada una respalda la tesis central.
